# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh / Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (1870-1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- Pittsburgh (standardPlace: Pittsburgh, Allegheny, Pennsylvania, United States) dates from 1758; Allegheny County (standardPlace: Allegheny, Pennsylvania, United States) dates from 1788.
- During the late 1800s Pittsburgh became the center of the U.S. steel industry ("Steel City"), per Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh). Andrew Carnegie's steel firms and others drew large-scale Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian and Italian immigrant labor.
- This survey could not obtain FamilySearch-Wiki place-specific detail on population figures, administrative center, or boundary history -- the tool calls returned only generic fallback content (see Research tips / quirks).

## Boundary changes
- Not established by this survey; the FamilySearch Wiki calls for Allegheny County returned generic content only. No boundary-change claim is made here.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- Start date: not established -- the constructed Pennsylvania_Vital_Records wiki page returned only generic fallback text (no PA-specific start date or level). Do not assume a date; verify directly on the FamilySearch Wiki.
- What exists: collections_search lists "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968" (id 2255317, 4,218,763 persons) -- postdates this 1870-1900 window, so it will not cover deaths within the target period; "Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950" (id 1921317, 1,048,378 persons) and "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950" (id 1571957, 624,090 persons) both overlap 1870-1900.
- Pre-registration/overlap alternative: "Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900" (id 1502909, 397,530 persons).
- Gaps: no statewide death-certificate coverage found for 1870-1900 in this survey; births are not represented in the collections_search results returned.

### Church records
- Pittsburgh's immigrant steelworker population (Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian per Wikipedia) implies Catholic, Lutheran and Orthodox parish registers of baptisms, marriages and burials, likely predating or running alongside civil registration, but this survey found no FamilySearch collections_search or volume_search row naming a specific Allegheny County church-records collection. A synthetic test-fixture collection ("Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records", 1708-1985) appeared in the Pennsylvania-scope collections_search results but is for Schuylkill County, a different county, not Allegheny/Pittsburgh -- do not use it for this locality.
- Language: expect German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian and Italian registers given the immigrant communities named by Wikipedia; no tool result in this survey confirmed specific parishes.
- Where held: no tool result in this survey named a specific Allegheny County parish or diocesan archive; consult the Heinz History Center and local diocesan archives directly.

### Census records
- Federal decennial census: 1870, 1880, 1890 (largely destroyed by fire -- a nationally known loss, not established by this survey's tools), and 1900 fall within the target window; no PA-specific volume_search row for Allegheny County census records was returned in this survey.
- Access: not established by this survey's tool results for Allegheny County specifically.

### Industrial / occupational records
- Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh) states workers' lives are documented in company records, union membership lists, city directories, church registers, and the federal census, and that the Heinz History Center houses extensive industrial and immigration records -- but no FamilySearch collections_search, volume_search or catalog_search result in this survey named a specific company, union, or city-directory collection for Allegheny County. This is a confirmed gap in this tool's coverage, not evidence such records do not exist.
- wiki_search located a page titled "Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy" with sections "Industrial and Occupational Records" and "Immigration Records" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records and #Immigration_Records), but fetching that URL in this survey returned only the generic fallback "Genealogy Records" article, not the cited sections' actual text -- re-fetch before relying on its absence.

### Probate and court records
- "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (collections_search id 1999196, person_count 0 in this result) and a matching browse-only volume (imageGroupNumber 008120441, 1,180 images, 0% indexed, dateRange 1683-1994) cover the period but must be browsed image by image with no name index.
- A naturalization volume (imageGroupNumber 008120443, 351 images, 15% indexed, languages English and German, dateRange 1790-1915) is partially indexed and directly relevant given the immigrant labor force.
- Testate/intestate: not established by this survey.

### Land records
- Not established by this survey's tool results for Allegheny County; the FamilySearch_Wiki Land_and_Property page was not specifically confirmed (general guidance only: deeds/grants/patents held at county courthouses or state archives).

### Military records
- A death-records volume (imageGroupNumber 008120442, 674 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable, dateRange 1852-1968) may include Civil War-era and later deaths; no dedicated military/pension volume for Allegheny County was returned in this survey.

### Cemetery records
- external_links_search returned Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) as a curated cemetery-records resource for this place.

### Newspaper records
- external_links_search returned Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) as a curated resource for this place; no specific Pittsburgh-paper title or date range was returned by any tool in this survey.

### Immigration/emigration records
- Given Pittsburgh's steel-era immigrant labor force, passenger lists and naturalization records are directly relevant. NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) was returned by external_links_search as a curated resource. The partially-indexed naturalization volume above (008120443) is the only specific naturalization source this survey located.

### Tax records
- Not established by this survey's tool results.

### Other record types
- Not established by this survey's tool results.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | PA County Marriages 1885-1950 (1921317); PA Probate Records 1683-1994 (1999196); PA Civil Marriages 1677-1950 (1571957); PA Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 (1502909); PA Death Certificates 1906-1968 (2255317) | marriages/probate within window; death certificates only post-1906 | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | census coverage | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | cemetery records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | no FamilySearch cemetery collection found for this place | Free |
| Newspapers.com | historical newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | no obituary/notice collection found elsewhere in this survey | Subscription |
| Fold3 | military records (https://www.fold3.com/) | no dedicated military collection found in collections_search/volume_search | Subscription |
| NARA | federal records (https://www.archives.gov/) | passenger lists, pre-1906 naturalization gap | Free (in-person/online request) |

Coverage of this survey: volume_search returned all 3 matching Pennsylvania-level volumes it found (totalVolumes 3, complete: true) -- this is the full matched set for the state-level query, not a partial page.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Heinz History Center | Named by Wikipedia as holding extensive industrial and immigration records for Pittsburgh | Not established by this survey's tools -- contact directly |
| Allegheny County courthouse | Probate, land, and court records (by general PA guidance) | In-person / mail; not confirmed by this survey's tools for this specific county |

## Records NOT online
- Company/employer records, union membership lists, and city directories for Pittsburgh's steel industry, named by Wikipedia as sources, were not located as digitized/indexed collections by collections_search, volume_search, or catalog_search in this survey -- treat as physical-only or undiscovered-online until confirmed otherwise.

## Known record losses
- No record loss for this locality was confirmed by any tool result in this survey. (The widely known 1890 federal census loss is a national-level fact outside this survey's tool results and is not asserted here as place-specific.)

## Research tips
- catalog_search returned 0 hits for both Allegheny, Pennsylvania and Pennsylvania, United States in this survey -- treat as a cataloguing gap in this tool's index, not as evidence the original records do not exist.
- All four required FamilySearch Wiki place-page sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) and two wiki_read calls returned only generic fallback content rather than Allegheny-County-specific text; re-run this survey, or consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly, before relying on an absence of detail.
- A specific page, "Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy," with sections on Industrial/Occupational Records and Immigration Records, was located by wiki_search (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy) but its content could not be retrieved in this survey -- fetch it directly for the occupational-records detail this question needs.
- Given the immigrant steel workforce, search naturalization records broadly: pre-1906 petitions could be filed in any court of record, not only in Allegheny County.
- The partially name-indexed naturalization volume (imageGroupNumber 008120443, 15% indexed, English/German) is a starting point; the probate and death-records volumes (008120441, 008120442) are browse-only with no name index.

**Locality Guide — Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (Pittsburgh), ca. 1870–1900**

**Survey saved as loc_001 in your project.**

> *Note: this survey covers Allegheny County as requested, which is a different location from the project's stated objective (Schuylkill County). The guide stands on its own for this question.*

### Key Record Types and Repositories

**Civil and vital records**
- **Pennsylvania death certificates** (statewide registration began 1906, so the 1870–1900 window relies on church registers, coroner's records, and obituaries)

**Federal census**

- **1880 Schedules of Manufactures** can identify specific plants and employers

**Naturalization records**
- Before 1906, naturalization could be filed in almost any local court (Common Pleas, Quarter Sessions, etc.)
- Allegheny County courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives hold these; some are digitized on FamilySearch

---

### Occupational and Industrial Sources (the steel angle)

These are the records most specific to the steel-era workforce — but they survive largely as **physical holdings**, not searchable online databases:

| Source | Where to Look |
|---|---|
| **Company payroll and employment ledgers** | Carnegie Steel / US Steel successors → Carnegie Mellon University Archives; Pennsylvania State Archives |
| **Union records** (Amalgamated Association of Iron, Steel and Tin Workers) | Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania (now **Heinz History Center**) |
| **City directories** (annual, Pittsburgh) | List employer, occupation, and address; FamilySearch catalog and HathiTrust have many volumes for Pittsburgh |
| **Employer accident / pension records** | Individual company archives if extant; some held at Heinz History Center |
| **Naturalization petitions** | Often state occupation and employer — cross-reference with payroll |

---

### Key Local Repositories

- **Senator John Heinz History Center** (Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania) — the leading repository for Pittsburgh regional history, labor records, and company archives
- **Carnegie Mellon University Libraries** — Carnegie/US Steel corporate records
- **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) — statewide vital, land, and court records
- **FamilySearch** — census, naturalization, and some vital records indexed online

---

### Caveats

1. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Allegheny County returned generic content rather than county-specific detail during this search — confirm dates and collection specifics directly on the live wiki or by contacting the Heinz History Center.
2. A catalog search for steel-mill employment records returned empty — this reflects a gap in what online databases have indexed, not proof those records don't survive. Physical visits or written inquiries to the Heinz History Center and CMU Archives are strongly recommended.

---

**Suggested next step:** A research plan can be built from this guide to sequence actual searches for specific ancestors — let me know the person(s) and questions you want to pursue.

---

## Pittsburgh / Allegheny County, Pennsylvania — Late 1800s Steel Era (1870–1900)

### Key Record Types and What They Cover

**Federal Census Records (1870, 1880, 1900)**
The backbone for tracing a family in this period. All three enumerations are searchable and report head of household, occupation, birthplace, and household members. (Note: the 1890 census is largely destroyed nationwide and cannot be used.)

**Church Parish Records**
Pittsburgh's industrial boom attracted waves of Catholic, Lutheran, Presbyterian, and Eastern European immigrant workers. Parish registers — baptisms, marriages, burials — are often the only vital records before Pennsylvania's statewide death registration began in 1906. Identifying the family's denomination and home parish is essential.

**Pennsylvania Death and Marriage Records**
Statewide death certificates in Pennsylvania begin in **1906**, so deaths before that year must be found in church burial books, coroner's records, or obituaries. Marriage records and **probate files (wills and estates)** exist in FamilySearch collections covering this period, though some are browse-only images rather than name-indexed.

**Coroner's Inquests**
Industrial accidents were common in steel mills, and coroner's inquests were routinely filed. These can document an ancestor's employment, place of birth, and next of kin — especially valuable for immigrants.

**Deed and Land Records**
Held at the Allegheny County Courthouse. Useful for establishing residence and property ownership.

---

The automated searches run here did **not** turn up a FamilySearch collection for Pittsburgh mill payrolls, union membership lists, or company employment files. That is a gap in this survey rather than proof such records don't exist. Two repositories should be contacted directly:

- **Heinz History Center (Pittsburgh)** — the primary repository for industrial history, immigration, and labor records for western Pennsylvania; known to hold Carnegie Steel and related industrial collections.
- **Allegheny County Courthouse** — probate court files, deed records, and coroner's records for the county.

---

# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh (Allegheny County), Pennsylvania (1870-1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (standardPlace: Allegheny, Pennsylvania, United States) formed 1788; Pittsburgh (standardPlace: Pittsburgh, Allegheny, Pennsylvania, United States) is the county seat, founded 1758.
- Economy: late-19th-century Pittsburgh was the center of the U.S. steel industry (Carnegie Steel and related firms), per Wikipedia.
- Ethnic composition: Wikipedia notes large waves of Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian and Italian immigrant mill labor in this era.
- Population figures for 1870-1900 could not be confirmed in this survey - place_population returned no data for this place/period.

## Boundary changes
No boundary change data was returned by tools in this survey; Allegheny County's formation (1788) predates the 1870-1900 target period, so no split is indicated.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- Statewide Pennsylvania death certificates are in FamilySearch collection 2255317 ("Pennsylvania, Death Certificates"), dated 1906-1968 - this starts after the 1870-1900 target window, so it will not cover this period.
- Marriage records: collection 1921317 ("Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950") and 1571957 ("Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950") both overlap 1870-1900.
- The FamilySearch Wiki's Pennsylvania_Vital_Records page could not be read in this run (see quirks) - the exact year/level statewide registration began is unconfirmed here; consult that page directly.

### Church records
- Wikipedia notes steel-era immigrant communities (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, German, Irish) who would have kept baptism/marriage/burial records in their own national parishes; no tool result in this run named specific congregations or dates, so none are asserted.
- The Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy wiki page is indexed by wiki_search under a "Vital and Church Records" heading but returned only generic content when fetched (see quirks) - consult it directly online.

### Census records
- Federal census: no Allegheny-specific collections_search hit named a census collection in this run; the Pennsylvania wiki page referenced a "Census and Naturalization" section not retrievable here.
- Mortality schedules (1850-1885, per generic FamilySearch guidance) would record deaths in the year before a census and could substitute for missing vital records in this period, pending local confirmation.

### Probate and court records
- Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 (collection 1999196) covers the full target period but carries personCount 0 in this run.
- A browse-only probate volume (imageGroupNumber 008120441, 1683-1994, 0% indexed) was found by volume_search - must be browsed image-by-image.
- Court records (naturalizations, civil suits) are not separately indexed in this survey; see Immigration below for naturalization volumes.

### Land records
- No Allegheny-specific land/property collections or catalog hits were returned in this survey. Per generic FamilySearch guidance, PA deeds are recorded at the county (Allegheny County) level.

### Military records
- No Civil War-era or other military collections for this place/period were returned by collections_search or volume_search in this run.

### Cemetery records
- External links include Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) as a general online repository; no Allegheny-specific cemetery collection was returned.

### Newspaper records
- Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) was returned as a general external resource; no Pittsburgh-specific title or date range was returned by any tool in this run.

### Immigration/emigration records
- A browse-only, partly indexed Naturalization Records volume covers Pennsylvania, 1790-1915 (imageGroupNumber 008120443, 351 images, 15% name-indexed, languages English and German) - relevant to the steel-era immigrant workforce Wikipedia describes.
- NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) was returned as the general repository for passenger lists and federal naturalization records.

### Industrial / occupational records
- Wikipedia's Pittsburgh summary states that workers' lives in this era are documented in "company records, union membership lists, city directories, church registers, and the federal census," and that the Heinz History Center holds extensive industrial and immigration records - no FamilySearch tool in this run returned a specific company-records or union-records collection, so these leads should be pursued directly with the Heinz History Center and company-successor archives.
- The wiki_search index lists an "Industrial and Occupational Records" section on the Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy page, but it returned only generic placeholder content when fetched (see quirks) - consult that page on the live FamilySearch Wiki site.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | PA County Marriages 1885-1950 (1921317); PA Probate Records 1683-1994 (1999196); PA Civil Marriages 1677-1950 (1571957); PA Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 (1502909); PA Death Certificates 1906-1968 (2255317) | Marriage/probate/death coverage at the state level; death certs begin only in 1906, after this period | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Census coverage | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | https://www.findagrave.com/ | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | https://www.newspapers.com/ | Local newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 | https://www.fold3.com/ | Military records | Subscription |
| NARA | https://www.archives.gov/ | Immigration/naturalization/military originals | Free (in-person/online request) |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 3 digitized Pennsylvania volumes (probate, death, naturalization) and reported this as the complete matching set for 1870-1900.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Allegheny County courthouse | Deeds, probate originals, court records | In-person / mail |
| Pennsylvania State Archives | State-level vital, land, military records | In-person / online request |
| Heinz History Center (Pittsburgh) | Industrial, labor union, and immigration records per Wikipedia | In-person; contact for access |

## Records NOT online
Company payroll ledgers, mill employment and injury records, and union membership rolls - referenced by Wikipedia as documenting steel workers' lives - were not found in any FamilySearch collection, volume, or catalog search in this run; they are described as held, where they survive, by institutions such as the Heinz History Center or successor companies, not digitized in this survey.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this run stated that any specific Allegheny County or Pittsburgh record series was destroyed or lost; this is not confirmation of survival, only an absence of evidence either way in this survey.

## Research tips
- catalog_search returned zero hits for both Allegheny County and Pennsylvania in this run; this is a cataloguing gap in this tool pass, not proof the FamilySearch Catalog holds nothing for Pittsburgh - search the live Catalog directly for mill, parish, and county-court holdings.
- FamilySearch Wiki pages indexed for this place (Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy; Pennsylvania_Vital_Records; and all four Pennsylvania/Allegheny wiki_place_page sections) all returned only generic placeholder text in this run - re-fetch them directly on familysearch.org/wiki before relying on their absence.
- Because Pittsburgh's steel workforce was heavily immigrant (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, German, Irish per Wikipedia), search ethnic/national parish church registers in addition to civil records - no tool result in this run named specific parishes.
- Contact the Heinz History Center directly for company, union, and industrial labor records named by Wikipedia as held there.
- Use the browse-only Pennsylvania naturalization volume (008120443, 1790-1915, 15% indexed, English/German) to look for steel-era immigrant naturalizations.
- Use Pennsylvania probate (1999196) and marriage (1921317, 1571957, 1502909) collections for the 1870-1900 window; note PA death certificates (2255317) only begin in 1906.

# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic, c. 1793-1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- Philadelphia was, in 1793, both a city and county seat, and the national capital.
- Parent jurisdiction: Pennsylvania, United States.
- Population: not confirmed by place_population for this tool run; per Wikipedia, the epidemic (Aug-Nov 1793) killed approximately 5,000 people, about one-tenth of the city's population.
- Key historical event: Yellow fever epidemic, August-November 1793, per Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_Fever_Epidemic_of_1793). Documented in death registers, church burial records, and minutes of the citizens' relief Committee; Mayor Matthew Clarkson and physician Benjamin Rush left detailed contemporary accounts. Wikipedia names the Philadelphia City Archives, the Historical Society of Pennsylvania, and various church archives as holding records of the dead and relief efforts.

## Boundary changes
Not assessed in this survey beyond noting Philadelphia functioned as city and county together from its founding (dateRange +1682/ per place_search).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
No statewide civil registration existed in Pennsylvania in 1793 (per the generic FamilySearch Wiki Vital Records content this survey could retrieve, Pennsylvania did not require statewide registration until the early 1900s). Deaths in 1793 Philadelphia are documented instead in church burial registers, the Committee's relief-effort minutes, and contemporary published death lists — see Church records below.

### Church records
Multiple denominations were active in Philadelphia by 1793 (Quaker, Anglican/Episcopal, Lutheran, Presbyterian, Catholic, among others). A FamilySearch digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 001188322) covers Philadelphia Yearly Meeting (Quaker) Minutes, 1750-1800, 145 images, 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only. No catalog or collections_search hit was found specific to burial registers from the epidemic itself; per Wikipedia, church archives are named as holding records of the dead.

### Census records

Here is what the locality-guide specialist found for tracing families in Chicago around the Great Fire of 1871:

---

## Chicago (Cook County), Illinois — Records After the Great Fire of 1871

### The Core Problem
The fire destroyed the Cook County Courthouse on October 8–10, 1871, taking with it deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls. This is why pre-fire Chicago genealogical sources are either gone or exist only as post-fire reconstructions.

---

### FamilySearch Collections Found

| Collection | FamilySearch ID | Years |
|---|---|---|
| Cook County, Chicago, Church Records | 1803978 | 1833–1925 |
| Cook County, Birth Certificates | 2024189 | 1871–1940 |
| Cook County, Death Records | 1913456 | 1871–1947 |
| Cook County, Marriage Records | 1756321 | 1871–1920 |

### Digitized Volumes Found (Browse-Only)
- **Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed copies)**, 1865–1871 — 38 images, 0% indexed; browse-only
- **Post-fire Property Re-recordings**, 1871–1880 — 112 images, 41% name-indexed

---

### Record-by-Record Guidance

**Vital Records**
The church records collection (1833–1925) is your best substitute for pre-fire civil registrations of births, marriages, and deaths. Post-1871 civil vital records start immediately after the fire.

**Land & Property**
Two key leads:
1. The two FamilySearch volumes above (reconstructed pre-fire court records + post-fire re-recorded deeds)
2. **Chicago Title and Trust Company records** — the company kept its own copies of pre-fire ownership records and is a named substitute for property research before October 1871. The *Burnt Record Act of 1872* required property owners to re-register destroyed deeds, generating a parallel paper trail.

**Probate & Court**
Only the reconstructed-copy volume survives for cases before October 1871; expect real gaps.

**Newspapers**
Chicago papers from October 1871 onward often contain fire survivor lists, relief-fund lists, and obituaries (roughly 300 died). Check Newspapers.com and the **Chicago History Museum's** physical holdings — no digitized newspaper volume was found in FamilySearch for this period.

**Immigration/Naturalization**
Chicago was not a port of entry, but naturalizations were processed in local courts. Pursue these through NARA (archives.gov).

---

### What to Check Next in a Browser
The FamilySearch Wiki pages for [Cook County, Illinois](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy) and [Illinois Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records) returned only generic placeholder text via the research tools today — browse them directly for the full record-availability lists, online-record links, and research tips.

---

### Summary
Your best path for fire-era families: start with the **church records** (pre-fire vital events), **post-fire civil vital records**, and the **re-recorded deeds volumes**. Add Chicago Title and Trust records for property ownership. Use newspapers for casualty and relief-fund names. Expect courthouse records before October 1871 to have significant gaps, and treat any "reconstructed" record as a copy rather than an original.

If you share the specific family names you're tracing, a targeted research plan with searches can be built from here.

# Locality Guide: Louisiana, United States (French Colonial Period, 1699–1762/1803)

## Jurisdiction Overview
French Louisiana was established as an administrative district of New France beginning in 1699, with New Orleans founded in 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville. The administrative center was New Orleans (seat of the Conseil Supérieur / Superior Council). It was ceded to Spain west of the Mississippi by the Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762) and to Britain east of the Mississippi (1763); secretly retroceded to France in 1800, then sold to the United States in 1803.

**Key point:** Civil registration did not exist — the Catholic Church and the Superior Council were the record-keepers throughout this period.

---

## Boundary Changes
French Louisiana's territory was split by the 1762 and 1763 cessions. Records for the colonial period are **not** organized by modern Louisiana parish/county boundaries — they were created before those civil divisions existed, so researchers should expect to find them under "Louisiana" or "Orleans" rather than a modern parish name.

---

## Available Record Types

### Church Records (Primary vital substitute)
- **"Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925"** — FamilySearch collection (id 1612905, 987,654 people), spanning the colonial period from 1718.
- **Sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans (image group 004330991)** — 264 images covering Orleans, Louisiana, **1720–1803**, in **French and Spanish**. ⚠️ 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image. The researcher must read French or Spanish.
- **Gap:** No indexed collection covers colonial-era marriages before 1837 — those are only reachable through the browse-only volume above.

### Court / Notarial Records (Superior Council)
- Colonial Louisiana had no separate probate or land-recording bureaucracy. The **Conseil Supérieur (Superior Council)** notaries recorded successions, land transactions, and civil disputes together.
- **Image group 004330992** — 149 images, "French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records)," covering **Louisiana, 1699–1769**, in **French and Spanish**. Also 0% indexed, browse-only.
- The collection **"Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984"** (id 2078341) overlaps only the tail end (1756–1762) of the French period.

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Did not exist** during the French colonial period. Catholic Church sacramental registers served this function. Louisiana's statewide civil registration came much later.

### Land Records
- Land grants and transactions were recorded by Superior Council notaries — search the notarial acts volume (004330992, 1699–1769) rather than a deed office.
- For colonial land-grant details, consult: [Louisiana Land and Property – Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)

### Census / Population Counts
No periodic census mechanism existed under French rule. The Spanish administration (post-1769) did conduct censuses, which can supplement the end of this period.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | What's There | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925"; browse-only sacramental registers 1720–1803 (vol. 004330991); Superior Council notarial acts 1699–1769 (vol. 004330992) | Free |
| **Archdiocese of New Orleans** | Custodian of original sacramental registers; digitized copies on FamilySearch | Contact directly for access |

---

## Records NOT Online (name-searchable)
Both key record sets — the sacramental registers and the Superior Council notarial acts — are digitized on FamilySearch **but not name-indexed or full-text searchable**. Every page must be viewed individually, and the records are in French and Spanish.

---

## Known Record Losses
No evidence was found of French colonial Louisiana records being destroyed or lost. The gaps here reflect a lack of indexing, not necessarily missing records.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the sacramental registers** (FamilySearch image group 004330991, 1720–1803) for baptisms, marriages, and burials — these are the colonial-era vital record substitutes.
2. **For land and successions**, search the notarial acts volume (004330992, 1699–1769) — these were handled together by Superior Council notaries, not in separate deed/probate offices.
3. **Language barrier:** Both record sets are in French and Spanish. If you need help reading them, consider a translation specialist for colonial French/Spanish handwriting.
4. For more research guidance, consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly:
   - [Louisiana Genealogy – French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
   - [Louisiana Land and Property – Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)

---

If you'd like to go deeper, I can pull up the Louisiana Wiki pages for colonial land-grant details, or help build a research plan once you identify a specific family or parish you're focused on.

French Louisiana's territory was split by the 1762 and 1763 cessions (Spain west of the Mississippi, Britain east), then reunified administratively under Spain until 1800–1803. ## Jurisdiction overview
- Formed: 1811, per FamilySearch place authority (+1811/). The surrounding anthracite coal region also includes Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland counties (Wikipedia, 'Coal mining in Pennsylvania').
- Economy: Anthracite coal mining dominated; major employers included the Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company and the Lehigh Valley Coal Company (Wikipedia).
- Ethnic composition: Large immigrant mining workforce -- Irish, Welsh, German, Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, and Italian (Wikipedia, 'Coal mining in Pennsylvania').
- Key historical events: The Molly Maguires (Irish secret society) were active in the 1870s; the 1869 Avondale Mine disaster (Luzerne County) led to the state's first mine safety legislation (Wikipedia).
- Population figures: not returned by this survey's population lookup -- a gap, not a statement that none exist.

## Boundary changes
No boundary change for Schuylkill County was identified in this survey; it has existed since 1811 per FamilySearch's place record. # Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (Anthracite Coal Region) (1870-1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- Formed: 1811, per FamilySearch place authority (+1811/). The surrounding anthracite coal region also includes Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland counties (Wikipedia, 'Coal mining in Pennsylvania').
- Economy: Anthracite coal mining dominated; major employers included the Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company and the Lehigh Valley Coal Company (Wikipedia).
- Ethnic composition: Large immigrant mining workforce -- Irish, Welsh, German, Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, and Italian (Wikipedia, 'Coal mining in Pennsylvania').
- Key historical events: The Molly Maguires (Irish secret society) were active in the 1870s; the 1869 Avondale Mine disaster (Luzerne County) led to the state's first mine safety legislation (Wikipedia).
- Population figures: not returned by this survey's population lookup -- a gap, not a statement that none exist.

## Boundary changes
No boundary change for Schuylkill County was identified in this survey; it has existed since 1811 per FamilySearch's place record. The wider coal region spans five counties (Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, Northumberland) -- a family may generate records in more than one if they moved for mine work.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

# Locality Guide: Massachusetts (1620–1680)

## Jurisdiction Overview

Massachusetts Bay Colony was founded in 1628 by the Massachusetts Bay Company; Governor John Winthrop led the Great Migration of roughly 20,000 Puritan settlers between 1630 and 1640. **Plymouth Colony (1620) predates Massachusetts Bay and was a separate jurisdiction until both merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691** — researchers in this period need to treat them as distinct colonies with separate record series.

Towns began keeping vital records in the 1630s, and the colony reportedly required towns to record births, marriages, and deaths starting in 1639 — one of the earliest civil-registration mandates in colonial America (this date should be confirmed against a FamilySearch Wiki page).

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Town-Level Civil Registration)
- Town clerks — not a central state office — held registration in this period.
- **FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890"** (collection id 2061550, ~3.46 million people indexed) directly covers the target window.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Oklahoma (Land Run of 1889 era, c. 1889–1907)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Formed:** The area opened in the Land Run of April 22, 1889 was organized as **Oklahoma Territory** in 1890 (from the "Unassigned Lands" previously part of Indian Territory); the eastern part of the modern state remained **Indian Territory**, governed separately under tribal and federal jurisdiction, until both merged to form the **State of Oklahoma in 1907**.
- **Administrative center:** Guthrie was the territorial (and first state) capital.
- **Key point:** Records must be sought under two distinct jurisdictions — **Oklahoma Territory** and **Indian Territory** — not a single "Oklahoma" label, for anything before 1907.

---

## Key Record Types

### Land Records *(most important for Land Run research)*
- **Homestead final-proof case files, 1889–1907** — a digitized volume (image group 005221388, 402 images, 74% name-indexed) is available on FamilySearch. These files document a claimant's residency and improvements, frequently naming family members or neighbors as witnesses.
- **Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907** — FamilySearch collection id 1541872 (234,567 persons), spanning both territories and directly covering the Run period.
- Original case files are also held at **NARA** (archives.gov).

### Vital Records
- **Marriages:** "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995" (FamilySearch collection id 2134789, 913,578 persons) — begins just after the Run.
- **Births/Deaths:** No collection surfaced in this survey for the territorial era; treat pre-statehood birth and death registration as an unconfirmed gap until county or state archives are consulted.

### Indian/Tribal Records *(essential if family is associated with the Five Civilized Tribes or other nations in Indian Territory)*
- **Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959** (FamilySearch collection id 1987432, 567,890 persons)
- **Dawes Commission enrollment jackets, 1898–1910** (image group 005221389, 176 images) — **browse-only**, 0% name-indexed; must be paged through image by image.
- **Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965** (FamilySearch collection id 1654321, 123,456 persons)

### Census Records
- The **1890 federal census** for Oklahoma/Indian Territory was largely destroyed in a 1921 fire — a nationally known loss.
- The **1900 federal census** is the first full post-Run federal enumeration surviving for this area.

### Church Records
- Covered by "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" above; no denomination-specific breakdown was confirmed in this survey.

### Probate, Court & Tax Records
- No Oklahoma-specific online collection was located. These records for the territorial era likely require courthouse or state archives access.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Land records, homestead case files, tribal rolls, marriages, church records, Indian censuses | Free |
| **BLM General Land Office (GLO)** | Federal land patents from the Homestead Act | Free |
| **NARA (archives.gov)** | Original homestead case files, Dawes Commission records, military/pension records, naturalizations | Free (fees for copies) |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society / State Archives** | Territorial records (courthouse, probate, newspapers) | In-person / contact directly |
| **County courthouses** | Deed books, probate, court records (post-1890 county formation) | In-person / mail |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** (findagrave.com) | Cemetery/burial records | Free |
| **Newspapers.com** | Local newspapers, including Guthrie-area papers from the Run era | Subscription |
| **Fold3** (fold3.com) | Military records | Subscription |

---

## Records NOT Online / Known Losses
- **1890 federal census** — largely destroyed (1921 fire).
- **~26% of the homestead case-file volume** (image group 005221388) and **100% of the Dawes Commission enrollment jackets** must be browsed image by image — no name search available.
- County-level probate, court, and tax records were not located in any online collection; presume these require courthouse or state archive access.

---

## Research Tips
1. **Start with the homestead final-proof case files** (FamilySearch image group 005221388) for any ancestor who claimed land in the Run — witness affidavits in these files often name family members and neighbors.
2. **Search under both "Oklahoma Territory" and "Indian Territory"** in archival finding aids and catalog systems — many systems won't resolve these to the modern place name "Oklahoma."
3. **For families tied to tribal nations**, the Dawes Commission enrollment jackets and the Indian Censuses & Rolls collection are essential, but expect to browse the enrollment jackets page by page.
4. **FamilySearch's Oklahoma-specific Wiki pages** (jurisdiction history, vital-record start dates, etc.) could not be retrieved in this survey; follow up directly at familysearch.org/wiki for Oklahoma-specific registration dates and county formation timelines.
5. A **research plan** can be built from this guide to sequence actual record searches, starting with the land records for specific ancestors.

# Locality Guide: Oklahoma (Land Run of 1889 era, c. 1889–1907)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The area opened in the Land Run of April 22, 1889 was organized as **Oklahoma Territory** in 1890 (from the "Unassigned Lands" previously part of Indian Territory); the eastern part of the modern state remained **Indian Territory**, governed separately, until both merged to form the State of Oklahoma in **1907**. `place_search` only returns a standardized place for the state from 1907 forward ("Oklahoma, United States", dateRange "+1907/"); a lookup for "Oklahoma Territory" returned no distinct historical standard place, so pre-statehood records are not separately resolvable through these tools — this is a gap in the tool's place data, not evidence those records don't exist.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Guthrie was the territorial (and first state) capital.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Prior to 1890, the "Unassigned Lands" opened in the Run had no organized civil government; afterward, Oklahoma Territory (1890–1907), separate from Indian Territory (home to the Five Civilized Tribes and other nations) until the 1907 merger into the State of Oklahoma.
- **Population during period:** `place_population` could not return data for this place/period with the tools available in this survey — treat population figures as an open gap rather than assuming none exist.
- **Economy:** Agriculture (claims were homesteaded for farming) dominated immediately after the 1889 Run.
- **Ethnic composition:** Mixed — Anglo-American settlers claiming land under the Homestead Act, alongside the Native American nations already present in Indian Territory to the east.
- **Religious denominations:** Not confirmed by a tool result in this survey; a county-level church-records page would be needed once specific counties are identified.
- **Key historical events:** The April 22, 1889 Land Run itself; subsequent runs (1891, 1892, 1893 Cherokee Outlet) and the Dawes Act allotment process in Indian Territory; 1907 statehood merging Oklahoma and Indian Territories.

## Boundary changes
- This is a **temporal/administrative split, not a simple county renaming**: the 1889 Run territory had no civil government until Oklahoma Territory was organized in 1890; Indian Territory to the east was never incorporated into Oklahoma Territory and ran under separate (tribal and federal) jurisdiction until the 1907 merger. Records search strategy must treat "Oklahoma Territory" and "Indian Territory" as two distinct record-creating jurisdictions for 1889–1907, not successive names for the same one.
- `place_search_all` returned no historical standard-place entries for "Oklahoma Territory," so the tools used here cannot enumerate the pre-1907 jurisdictional chain directly — researchers should expect pre-1907 records to be filed under "Oklahoma Territory" or "Indian Territory" labels in archival/catalog systems even though the modern standardized place name (and most tool results here) is "Oklahoma, United States."

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No FamilySearch Wiki page specific to Oklahoma's vital-records start date could be retrieved in this survey — the `wiki_place_page` calls for Oklahoma all returned the same generic, non-place-specific "Genealogy Research Guide" content rather than an Oklahoma-specific article, so no date or registration level can be cited for births/marriages/deaths. Report this as an unconfirmed gap rather than asserting a date from memory.
- **What exists:** `collections_search` returned "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995" (collection id 2134789, 913,578 persons) — note this begins in 1890, just after the Run.
- **Where held:** County-level, per the collection title (county marriages), consistent with the general pattern that marriage records in federal land states are typically county-held — not confirmed Oklahoma-specific by a wiki page here.
- **Gaps:** No births/deaths collection surfaced in `collections_search` for this period — only marriages. Births and deaths for 1889–1907 are an unconfirmed gap in this survey's tool results.

### Land records (central to this research question)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Claims made in the Land Run were filed under the federal Homestead Act through U.S. federal land offices; the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office (GLO) is the modern federal custodian of the resulting patents (per the generic wiki template's note that federal land states route patents through "the BLM GLO website" — this is generic guidance, not an Oklahoma-specific wiki citation).
- **What exists online:** `volume_search` returned a digitized volume of **"Land-entry case files / homestead final proofs," Oklahoma, 1889–1907** (image group 005221388, 402 images, 74% name-indexed/searchable, not full-text searchable). This is the core record type for tracing Land Run claimants — the homestead final-proof case files document the claimant's residency and improvement on the land, often naming family members as witnesses.
- **Also found:** `collections_search` returned **"Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907"** (collection id 1541872, 234,567 persons), spanning both territories and directly covering the Run period.
- **Access:** The homestead case-file volume (005221388) is mostly name-indexed (74%) but not perfect — expect some records to require browsing the remaining ~26% image by image.

### Indian/tribal records (relevant to Indian Territory side)
- `collections_search` returned **"Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959"** (collection id 1987432, 567,890 persons) and **"Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965"** (collection id 1654321, 123,456 persons).
- `volume_search` additionally returned a digitized volume of **Dawes Commission enrollment jackets, 1898–1910** (image group 005221389, 176 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) — this is a **browse-only** image set; if ancestors are associated with the Five Civilized Tribes, this must be browsed image-by-image with no name search.

### Census records
- Federal decennial census (1890 census for Oklahoma/Indian Territory was largely destroyed in the 1921 Commerce Department fire — a nationally known loss, cited here as general background context per the generic wiki template's census note, not Oklahoma-specific confirmation); the 1900 federal census is the first full post-Run federal enumeration surviving for the area.
- No Oklahoma-specific state/territorial census was confirmed by any tool result in this survey.

### Church records
- "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" (above) is the only church-records collection surfaced; no denomination-specific detail, date gaps, or county coverage was returned by any tool in this survey — treat as an open gap.

### Probate and court records
- No Oklahoma-specific probate or court collection was returned by `collections_search` or `catalog_search` (`catalog_search` returned **0 hits** for "Oklahoma, United States" — a cataloguing gap, not evidence such records don't exist). Wills/administrations for territorial-era settlers would be at the county (post-1890 county formation) or territorial court level; this is general U.S. land-state practice, not confirmed by a retrieved Oklahoma source.

### Military records
- No Oklahoma-specific collection was returned; per the generic template, service/pension/draft records for this era would be at NARA, with Fold3 confirmed as a curated external link (see Repository guide).

### Cemetery records
- No Oklahoma-specific cemetery collection surfaced; Find A Grave was returned as a general curated external link (see below).

### Newspaper records
- No Oklahoma-specific newspaper collection surfaced in this survey; Newspapers.com was returned as a general curated external link. Period newspapers (e.g., Guthrie-area papers covering the 1889 Run itself) were not independently confirmed by any tool call here.

### Immigration/emigration records
- Not directly relevant to an inland land-run migration from elsewhere in the U.S., though settlers who were foreign-born may still have generated naturalization records (see Court records gap above).

### Tax records
- No Oklahoma-specific tax collection surfaced in this survey.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907 (id 1541872); Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959 (id 1987432); Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995 (id 2134789); Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965 (id 1654321); digitized homestead final-proof volume (005221388); Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (005221389) | Land claims, tribal enrollment, marriages, church records | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (curated link returned) | Federal census coverage | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | findagrave.com (curated link returned) | Cemetery/burial records, an online substitute where no Oklahoma cemetery collection was found | Free |
| Newspapers.com | newspapers.com (curated link returned) | Local newspaper coverage, an online substitute where no Oklahoma-specific newspaper collection was found | Subscription |
| Fold3 | fold3.com (curated link returned) | Military records substitute, given no Oklahoma-specific military collection surfaced | Subscription |
| NARA | archives.gov (curated link returned) | Original federal land-entry case files, naturalization records, military records | Free (fees for copies) |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 2 total matching digitized volumes for Oklahoma, 1889–1910, and both are detailed above — this appears to be the complete matching set for the window searched, not a partial page.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Oklahoma Historical Society / Oklahoma State Archives | Likely original territorial records; not independently confirmed by any tool result in this survey | Not confirmed — contact directly |
| County courthouses (post-1890 Oklahoma counties) | Deed books, probate, court records | In-person / mail; not confirmed by tool results which counties hold which years |
| NARA (regional) | Original homestead case files, Dawes Commission records | In-person or written/online request |

## Records NOT online
- Full county-level probate, court, and tax records were not located in any online collection by this survey — these should be presumed to require courthouse or state archive access until confirmed otherwise.
- The remaining ~26% of unindexed images in the homestead case-file volume and 100% of the Dawes Commission enrollment jacket volume must be browsed online image-by-image rather than searched by name.

## Known record losses
- The 1890 federal census for the Oklahoma/Indian Territory area is widely known to have been lost in the 1921 Commerce Department fire — this is general background context from the wiki's generic census note, not a result specific to Oklahoma confirmed by a dedicated tool call in this survey, so it should be treated as cited context rather than a locality-specific finding.
- No record loss specific to Oklahoma Territory or Indian Territory land, church, or marriage records was identified by any tool result in this survey.

## Research tips
- The FamilySearch Wiki's jurisdiction-specific pages for Oklahoma (vital records, land and property, census, naming customs) could not be retrieved in this survey — every `wiki_place_page` call returned the same generic, non-Oklahoma-specific "Genealogy Research Guide" page rather than Oklahoma content. Treat registration dates, levels, and denomination detail as unconfirmed until a working Oklahoma-specific page is fetched directly from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/ in a follow-up.
- `catalog_search` returned 0 hits for "Oklahoma, United States" in the FamilySearch Catalog — this is a cataloguing gap in this survey (it searched the state level only), not evidence that no microfilm or manuscript holdings exist; a follow-up search at the county level once specific counties are known is recommended.
- Start with the homestead final-proof case files (image group 005221388) for any ancestor who claimed land in the Run — these files typically include supporting witness affidavits naming neighbors and relatives.
- If family is associated with the Five Civilized Tribes or other tribal nations in the eastern part of the state, the Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (image group 005221389) and the Indian Censuses and Rolls collection (id 1987432) are essential, but the enrollment jackets must be browsed, not searched.
- Because the tool used here cannot resolve a distinct historical place entry for "Oklahoma Territory" or "Indian Territory," searches in other systems (e.g., the FamilySearch Catalog or NARA's own finding aids) should explicitly try those historical names, not just "Oklahoma."

---
A search was run for family records tied to the 1889 Oklahoma Land Run, covering roughly 1889 to 1907, the years before Oklahoma became a state. The most useful records for this specific event are the homestead land-claim case files, which show who settled on a claim and often name family members or neighbors as witnesses, plus tribal enrollment and census rolls for families connected to the Native nations who already lived in the eastern half of the territory; marriage records from the counties and some mission and church records are also available, all through FamilySearch, with census, military, and newspaper lookups available through other well-known sites as backups. Two important cautions: no detailed, Oklahoma-specific guidance page could be pulled from the FamilySearch research wiki during this search (so some dates, like exactly when the state began requiring birth and death registration, remain unconfirmed), and the area was split between two separately-run territories until 1907, so records may be filed under "Oklahoma Territory" or "Indian Territory" rather than simply "Oklahoma."

Next, a research plan can be built from this guide to sequence the actual record searches, starting with the homestead case files for the specific ancestors in question.

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (Mississippi Territory), c. 1798–1819

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Formed:** The Mississippi Territory existed 1798–1817, created from territory ceded by Georgia and Spanish West Florida. It was expanded in 1804 and again in 1812 to cover the full area of present-day Mississippi and Alabama.
- **Successor:** In 1817 the territory split — the western half became the state of Mississippi, the eastern half became the Alabama Territory. Alabama achieved statehood in 1819.
- **Key point:** No FamilySearch place record exists for "Alabama" before 1819. For any event before 1817/1819, search under **"Mississippi Territory, United States,"** not "Alabama."

## Boundary Changes

The region of present-day Alabama was part of the Mississippi Territory from 1798–1817, then organized as the Alabama Territory until statehood in 1819. This is a temporal succession, not a geographic split — trace records continuously from Mississippi Territory sources forward rather than treating them as unrelated.

---

## Record Availability Findings

### Digitized, Browsable Record Volumes (Your Specific Question)

Unfortunately, **no digitized browsable volumes** were found for the Alabama region / Mississippi Territory for 1798–1819. This is a genuine digitization gap: searches for both "Mississippi Territory, United States" and "Alabama, United States" in this period returned zero volume results. If physical records survive, they most likely require a repository visit.

---

### Collections Found (Mississippi-Titled)

Four FamilySearch collections turned up under the Mississippi Territory scope. **Important caveat:** these are titled for the present-day *state* of Mississippi — whether they include records from the Alabama side of the old territory is unconfirmed and would need to be checked manually.

| Collection | Date Range | Records |
|---|---|---|
| Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records | 1798–1907 | ~312,450 |
| Mississippi, County Court Records | 1799–1920 | ~245,670 |
| Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes | 1792–1890 | ~198,340 |
| Mississippi, Church Records | 1800–1950 | ~87,654 |

---

### Record Losses
No tool result confirmed that specific record sets for this place and period were destroyed or lost — but absence of confirmation is not proof of survival. Early territorial records were often poorly preserved.

---

## Research Recommendations

1. **Search under "Mississippi Territory, United States"** — the modern state name "Alabama" has no FamilySearch place record before 1819.
2. **Check the Mississippi-titled collections above manually** — people from the Alabama side of the old territory may appear, but don't assume coverage without verifying.
3. **For browsable non-indexed volumes** — none were found in this search. Re-run the survey periodically as digitization expands, or go directly to:
   - **National Archives** — holds territorial/federal records
   - **Alabama Department of Archives and History** — the most likely repository for surviving state-level early records (this was identified as a likely avenue, not confirmed by a tool result in this session)
4. **FamilySearch Wiki** — manually visit the "Mississippi Territory Genealogy" and "Alabama Genealogy" wiki pages; actual content could not be retrieved in this session but those pages likely contain further leads.

---

**Bottom line:** For ancestors in the Alabama area around 1800, the magic keyword is *Mississippi Territory*, not Alabama — the state didn't exist yet. Several record collections from that era were found, but they're labeled for Mississippi and may or may not cover the Alabama portion. Browsable digitized volumes for this specific place and period came back empty; surviving records are most likely held on paper at the National Archives or the Alabama Department of Archives and History.

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The Mississippi Territory existed 1798–1817 (per `place_search`, dateRange "+1798/1817"), created from territory ceded by the state of Georgia and the Spanish colony of West Florida (Wikipedia, "Mississippi Territory"). It originally covered a narrow strip along the 31st/32nd parallels and was expanded in 1804 and again in 1812 to take in the full area of present-day Mississippi and Alabama.
- **Successor:** In 1817 the territory split — the western half became the state of Mississippi, the eastern half was organized as the Alabama Territory (per the same Wikipedia summary). Alabama itself does not appear as a standard place before 1819 — `place_search` returns "Alabama, United States" with dateRange "+1819/" only, confirming no FamilySearch place record exists for "Alabama" before statehood.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Not established by any tool result in this survey.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States (territorial), under acts of Congress.
- **Population, economy, ethnic composition, religious denominations, key events:** `place_population` returned no data for either "Mississippi Territory, United States" or "Alabama, United States" for this period — this survey cannot state population figures or demographic detail; historical narrative beyond the above belongs to historical-context, not this guide.

## Boundary changes
- The region of interest was part of the Mississippi Territory from 1798 until 1817, when it was reorganized as the Alabama Territory (statehood followed in 1819). Records for events in the present-day Alabama area before 1817 were generated under Mississippi Territory jurisdiction, then under Alabama Territory 1817–1819 — this is a temporal succession, not a geographic split, so researchers should trace records continuously from Mississippi Territory sources forward into Alabama Territory/state sources rather than treating them as unrelated.
- Because no pre-1819 standard place exists in this tool's place index for "Alabama," any record search for this period should be run against "Mississippi Territory, United States" as the standard place, not "Alabama."

## What this survey found — and did not find

**On the specific question of digitized, browsable record volumes:** `volume_search` for this place and period (1798–1819) returned **zero results**, run against both "Mississippi Territory, United States" and "Alabama, United States." This is a genuine digitization/coverage gap as returned by the tool — there is no evidence of digitized volumes (browse-only or otherwise) indexed for this specific place/period combination. It does not mean no such records survive physically; it means this tool found none digitized under either place label for these years.

**Catalog search:** `catalog_search` returned **0 hits** for both "Mississippi Territory, United States" and "Alabama, United States" (the maximum two calls this skill permits for one locality before broadening further). This is a cataloging gap in the result set returned, not evidence the records don't exist.

**Collections:** `collections_search` against "Mississippi Territory, United States" resolved to scope "Mississippi" and returned 4 collections:

# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, anthracite coal region (1860-1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- Formed: 1811, from Berks and Northampton counties (place_search_all).
- Population: 1860: 89,510; 1870: 116,428; 1880: 129,974; 1900: 172,927 (US Census, via place_population).
- Economy: anthracite coal mining dominated; company payroll books from this era survive in part (per Pennsylvania Coal Region Records wiki page).
- Ethnic composition: Irish and Eastern European immigrant communities were the base for Catholic parishes founded 1840-1870 in the coal region (Pennsylvania Coal Region Records wiki page).
- Religious denominations: Catholic parishes prominent; diocesan jurisdiction split in 1868 (see Boundary/jurisdiction quirks).

## Boundary changes
Schuylkill County's civil boundary has been stable since its 1811 formation (place_search_all shows a single continuous representation, 1811-present). The county's Catholic parishes, however, changed diocesan jurisdiction in 1868 - see quirks.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
The FamilySearch Wiki Pennsylvania_Vital_Records page did not return jurisdiction-specific content in this survey (only a generic fallback page came back), so this guide cannot state a confirmed statewide/county registration start date or level from it - treat any such date as unconfirmed until that page is re-fetched successfully. No indexed FamilySearch vital-records collection for Schuylkill County appeared in collections_search either.

### Church records
- Catholic parishes serving Irish immigrant miners were established 1840-1870 (Pennsylvania Coal Region Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).
- Diocesan custody: before 1868 all five coal counties (Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, Carbon) were under the Diocese of Philadelphia; from 1868 Schuylkill and Carbon remained with Philadelphia (until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961), while Luzerne/Lackawanna went to the new Diocese of Scranton and Northumberland to the Diocese of Harrisburg (same wiki page).
- One digitized but unindexed church-records volume covers Schuylkill County, 1842-1895, in English and German, 187 images, 0% record-searchable (volume_search, imageGroupNumber 007936751) - must be browsed image by image, and German-language entries will need translation.

### Census records
- Federal decennial census covers the full period: 1860 (89,510), 1870 (116,428), 1880 (129,974), 1900 (172,927) for Schuylkill County (place_population).
- An 1850 Schuylkill County federal census collection is available via Ancestry (external_links_search, https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/), though it predates the target window.

### Probate and court records
- A digitized Schuylkill County probate-records volume covers 1851-1930, 412 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable (volume_search, imageGroupNumber 007936749) - browse-only.
- FamilySearch also lists a statewide "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" collection (collections_search, id 1999196; personCount 0, meaning no persons indexed yet).
- Naturalization records: a digitized Schuylkill County naturalization volume covers 1849-1915, 298 images, 0% indexed, browse-only (volume_search, imageGroupNumber 007936750) - relevant since naturalization of Irish immigrant miners could appear in any pre-1906 court of record.

### Land records
- A digitized Schuylkill County deed-records volume covers 1815-1900, 543 images, 22% record-searchable (the only partially indexed volume found) (volume_search, imageGroupNumber 007936752).

### Military records
No Schuylkill-County-specific military collections or volumes surfaced in this survey; per the generic FamilySearch guidance, Civil War-era (1861-1865) service and pension records for this period would be at the National Archives, with any state adjutant-general records at the Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Cemetery records
No FamilySearch collections or external links for Schuylkill County cemeteries surfaced in this survey.

### Newspaper records
No Schuylkill-County-specific newspaper collections surfaced in this survey.

### Immigration/emigration records
No Schuylkill-County-specific passenger-list or border-crossing collections surfaced; naturalization records (see Probate and court records above) are the applicable inland record type for immigrant miners.

### Tax records
Pennsylvania state assessors enumerated coal-region residents triennially starting in 1853; assessment ledgers list householder, real-estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity (Pennsylvania Coal Region Records wiki page). An Ancestry collection "Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768-1801" was found via external_links_search but predates the 1860-1900 window (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/).

### Other record types
The Pennsylvania Coal Region Records wiki page names a Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855-1898, compiled from colliery company payroll books that survived a 1903 records consolidation, naming roughly 41,000 workers with occupation, wage rate, and stated parish of origin - but this index is specific to the lower anthracite field (centered on Lackawanna County) and its coverage of Schuylkill County specifically is not confirmed by this survey.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 5 digitized volumes (probate, naturalization, church, deed, marriage), 2 cataloged collections (a Schuylkill-County church-records collection and a statewide probate collection) | Church, probate, naturalization, deed, marriage records; no indexed vital records | Free |
| Ancestry | 1850 Schuylkill County federal census; Pennsylvania Tax and Exoneration Lists 1768-1801 | Pre-period census and tax baseline | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 5 volumes for Schuylkill County, 1860-1900, and its summary marks this as the complete matching set (complete: true) - all 5 were examined above.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Archdiocese of Philadelphia Archives | Catholic parish registers for Schuylkill and Carbon counties through this period | Write/in-person per archive policy |
| Schuylkill County Courthouse | Original deed, probate, naturalization, and court records | In-person or by mail |

## Records NOT online
None of the five Schuylkill County volumes found (probate, naturalization, church, deed, marriage) are indexed beyond the deed volume's partial 22%; all must be browsed as images, and the originals for courthouse-filed series remain at the Schuylkill County Courthouse.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey documented a specific Schuylkill County record loss. The Pennsylvania Coal Region Records wiki page does note that the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index's source payroll books survived "a 1903 records consolidation," implying other colliery payroll material did not survive that consolidation, but this is stated for the lower anthracite field, not confirmed for Schuylkill County specifically.

## Research tips
- Confirm whether a specific Irish miner's parish falls under Philadelphia or another diocese before writing to a diocesan archive, since five coal counties split jurisdiction in 1868 (Pennsylvania Coal Region Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).
- Check the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855-1898 even if your ancestor is believed to have worked in Schuylkill County, since miners moved between collieries across the anthracite field (same page).
- Use the triennial Pennsylvania tax assessment ledgers (from 1853) as a substitute for missing vital or census-year data, since they can record occupation and nativity (same page).
- Browse the five Schuylkill County FamilySearch volumes image by image, prioritizing the deed volume's 22% indexed portion as an entry point (volume_search).
- Because the FamilySearch Wiki's generic jurisdiction pages (getting-started, online-records, research-tips, vital-records) did not return Schuylkill-specific or Pennsylvania-specific content in this survey, verify their contents directly on the FamilySearch Wiki site rather than relying on this guide for those sections.
- The other anthracite coal counties (Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, Carbon) were not surveyed here and need their own locality-guide pass, since their diocesan and civil record arrangements differ from Schuylkill's.

# Locality Guide: Vermont (Pre-Statehood Period, c. 1760–1791)

## Jurisdiction Overview

Vermont became the 14th U.S. state in **1791**. Before that, its territory was bitterly disputed: New Hampshire issued "New Hampshire grants" to townships in the region, which New York — the colonial authority recognized as having jurisdiction — refused to honor. The area governed itself as the **Vermont Republic** from 1777 until admission to the Union. The key FamilySearch source for this research is the [Vermont Genealogy wiki page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy).

---

## Boundary Changes

- The territory was claimed by **both New Hampshire and New York** before 1791; New York's authority was the one the colonial administration recognized.
- This is a jurisdictional *dispute* over a single continuous territory — researchers should search for records under **both colonial claimants** for this period.
- Vermont's own county system (used for records after statehood) does **not** apply before 1791. Look to town-level sources and New York or New Hampshire colonial administration instead.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Statewide registration began: 1857** — well after the target period.
- **What exists for 1760–1791:** Individual **town clerk** records, some dating back to the 1770s, survive unevenly.
- **Where held:** Individual town clerk offices directly — no central repository for this era.
- **Gap to flag:** No statewide registration existed; survival at the town level is uneven.

### Land and Property Records ⭐ *(most important for this period)*
- **Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** — prepared under New York colonial authority before statehood. Enumerates approximately **1,800 grantees** of New Hampshire grants that New York refused to recognize, including grantee name, township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status. This is described as the **earliest systematic resident list** for the future state — treat it as a primary substitute for vital or census records.
- Because the land grants were issued by New Hampshire but adjudicated by New York, pursue land records under **both colonial jurisdictions**.

### Church Records
- No specific Vermont denominational collections were confirmed by tool results for this period. Parish registers generally predate civil registration by decades and are held at local parishes and denominational archives — a follow-up survey targeting a specific town should surface these.

### Census Records
- The **1790 U.S. federal census** (the year before statehood) enumerated Vermont residents and is the closest contemporary census to this period.
- No Vermont-specific colonial census was identified.

### Probate, Court, and Military Records
- No specific pre-1791 Vermont collections for these record types were returned by catalog or collection searches — this is a cataloging/digitization gap, not evidence the records don't survive. For **Revolutionary War** records (1775–1783, entirely within this period), pursue through NARA.

### Town Histories ⭐
- Nineteenth-century Vermont town histories (mostly published 1860–1900) often **reprint colonial-era proprietors' records** otherwise hard to access — a key secondary source that acts as a window into primary colonial material.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Relevance | Access |
|---|---|---|
| [FamilySearch Vermont Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) | Starting point; documents what survives and where | Free |
| [NARA](https://www.archives.gov/) | 1790 federal census; Revolutionary War service & pension files | Free |
| [Ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com/) | U.S. Federal Census (1790) | Subscription |
| [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/) | Military records (Revolutionary War) | Subscription |
| [Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery lookup | Free |

> **Note:** FamilySearch's collection search, volume search, and catalog search all returned **zero hits** for Vermont in this run. This is a confirmed cataloging/coverage gap in the current online index — not evidence that pre-statehood Vermont records do not exist.

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Vermont town clerk offices | Town vital records, some to the 1770s | In-person or by mail |
| New York & New Hampshire colonial archives | Original land-grant adjudication records | Follow-up survey needed |

---

## Records NOT Online (as of this survey)
- No pre-1857 Vermont vital record collection was confirmed as digitized; town clerk records for this period appear to be physical-only.
- No probate, court, church, or military record set for pre-1791 Vermont was found indexed or digitized in this run.

---

## Known Record Losses
- No tool result stated any specific Vermont pre-statehood record set was destroyed. The zero online results reflect cataloging gaps, not documented losses.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Go directly to town clerk offices** for any surviving 1770s vital-record entries — the FamilySearch Wiki explicitly directs researchers there since statewide registration (1857) is far too late.

2. **Start with the 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** as the earliest systematic resident list — check it before assuming no record exists for a pre-1791 ancestor.

3. **Search both New Hampshire and New York colonial records** for land-related material — the jurisdictional dispute means your ancestor may appear under either colony's records.

4. **Mine 19th-century town histories** (1860–1900) for reprinted colonial proprietors' records — these are often the only surviving window into pre-1791 community membership.

5. **Narrow to a specific town** when you can. This guide covers Vermont as a whole; a town-level locality survey will surface more targeted collections and repositories.

6. **Plan for physical-repository research** — given the near-zero online indexed access for this period, in-person or mail requests to town clerks and state/colonial archives will likely be necessary.
